title: Input
body:
[[Buffered Input]]

`cin`, from `#include <iostream>`. The `>>` operator reads one whitespace-delimited token and
converts it to the variable's type.

```c++
int age;
cout << "Age: ";
cin >> age;
```

The two habits that avoid most input bugs:

- **`>>` stops at whitespace.** Reading a name with `cin >> name` gets the first word only.
  `getline(cin, name)` takes the whole line, and mixing the two leaves a newline sitting in the
  buffer that the next `getline` reads as an empty string. That is [[Buffered Input]], and it
  is the thing that makes input feel haunted.
- **`>>` can fail.** Type a letter where an `int` was expected and the stream goes into a fail
  state and stops reading anything at all, which looks like an [[Infinite loop]] if the read is
  inside one. `if (cin >> age)` tests it.

`cin.get(ch)` reads one [[Character]], whitespace included, which is how [[C-String]]s get read
by hand. `cin.eof()` is true when input runs out, and is the [[Sentinel]] the course uses for
reading a [[File]] to the end.
